# Executive Summary

This collaborative course project explores reported base salaries in the global
Data Science and AI workforce using an **August 3, 2025** snapshot of the
aijobs.net salary dataset. The supplied dataset contains 151,445 rows;
removing exact row duplicates leaves **71,913 distinct records**. Because
respondent identifiers are unavailable, distinct rows should not be
interpreted as verified unique individuals.

We examine salary distributions across career stages and technical role
families, then estimate an adjusted association between remote status and
log salary. Median salaries generally rise by experience level. The adjusted
fully remote coefficient corresponds to an estimated **-0.7%** salary
difference relative to on-site work (**p = 0.141**), which is not
statistically distinguishable from zero at the 5% level. This does **not**
prove that the two groups receive equal pay or establish a causal effect.

The original assignment used **Walmart Global Tech as a hypothetical
prospective recruiting client**, not as an actual client or an employer whose
pay was directly observed. Company-specific recommendations are illustrative
and require independent evidence before real-world use.

**Explore the [interactive Shiny dashboard](https://4e3w5f-gaku-aihara.shinyapps.io/Libeccio_Career_Dashboard/)**
for role-family filters, experience-level comparisons, and career progression
summaries. Its underlying source code is not part of this report repository.

# 3 Core Questions

Using our data we aim to answer these core questions:

1. **How do reported compensation levels differ across Entry, Mid, Senior,
   and Executive positions?**

2. **Is fully remote status associated with a salary premium or penalty
   after adjusting for observed covariates?**

3. **How do salaries differ by role and employer size, and how does the
   partial-2025 snapshot compare with 2024?**

# 1. Data Scope and Credibility

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,

  fig.align = "center",

library(tidyverse)
```

```{r load-data, echo=FALSE}
# By default, read the course-provided snapshot. A local copy can be placed
# at data/salaries.csv.gz for offline rendering if its terms permit reuse.
source_url <- paste0(
  "https://stat.cmu.edu/~sgallagh/courses/mads-fall-2026/",
  "datavis-36613/data/salaries.csv.gz"
)
source_file <- "data/salaries.csv.gz"
salaries <- readr::read_csv(
  if (file.exists(source_file)) source_file else source_url,
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

## What does one row represent?

Each row is one reported compensation record for a single
job/person-year combination, self-submitted to the aijobs.net survey. It
is not a job posting, not a hire event, and there is no employer name,
posting ID, observation date, or row-level source to verify any
individual record. The raw dataset contains 151,445 observations across
11 variables.

## Exact duplicates

```{r duplicates, echo=FALSE}
# Create the exact-deduplicated analysis sample
salaries_no_duplicates <- salaries |>
  distinct()

# Summarize the duplicate audit
duplicate_audit <- tibble(
  measure = c(
    "All supplied records",
    "Exact-deduplicated records",
    "Repeated copies removed",
    "Share removed"
  ),
  value = c(
    comma(nrow(salaries)),
    comma(nrow(salaries_no_duplicates)),
    comma(nrow(salaries) - nrow(salaries_no_duplicates)),
    percent(
      1 - nrow(salaries_no_duplicates) / nrow(salaries),
      accuracy = 0.1
    )
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  duplicate_audit,
  col.names = c("Audit Measure", "Value"),
  caption = "Exact-duplicate audit"
)

# Compare experience-tier medians before and after deduplication
duplicate_sensitivity <- bind_rows(
  salaries |>
    mutate(sample = "All supplied records"),
  salaries_no_duplicates |>
    mutate(sample = "Exact duplicates removed")
) |>
  mutate(
    experience_level = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(sample, experience_level) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    n = comma(n),
    median_salary = dollar(median_salary, accuracy = 1)
  )

knitr::kable(
  duplicate_sensitivity,
  col.names = c("Sample", "Experience Level", "Count (n)", "Median Salary (USD)"),
  caption = "Sensitivity of experience-tier salary medians to duplicate handling"
)

# Set primary analysis sample
salaries_analysis <- salaries_no_duplicates
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    experience_level = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = experience_level, y = salary_in_usd)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.2, fill = "slategray2") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = dollar) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported salary rises across experience tiers after exact de-duplication",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Unique exact records only; n = 71,913. Salary is annual nominal USD,",
      "not total compensation or cost-of-living adjusted."
    ),
    x = "Experience level",
    y = "Annual salary in USD (log scale)",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net global salary survey snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Exact duplicates removed."
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The dataset contained 151,445 supplied compensation records. Removing
exact duplicate rows left 71,913 unique records, meaning that 52.5% of
supplied rows were repeated copies of an identical record. Because the
archive has no respondent ID, employer name, posting ID, or row-level
provenance, we cannot determine whether those repeated rows are data
duplicates or distinct respondents with identical observed
characteristics. We wanted to prevent potentially repeated observations
from receiving extra weight, and we want to reduce the risk of
overstating the amount of information in the dataset. Therefore, we use
the exact de-duplicated dataset ($n = 71,913$) for our primary analysis.

## Missingness and Currency Standardization

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Missingness audit across all 11 variables
missing_audit <- salaries_analysis |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing_Count") |>
  mutate(Missing_Pct = percent(Missing_Count / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.1))

knitr::kable(
  missing_audit,
  col.names = c("Variable Name", "Missing Values (NA)", "Missing Share"),
  caption = "Field-level missingness audit across deduplicated records (n = 71,913)"
)

# Currency breakdown (Top 5)
currency_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  count(salary_currency, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  currency_summary,
  col.names = c("Currency Code", "Record Count", "Share of Total"),
  caption = "Top reporting currencies prior to USD normalization"
)

```

Across all 11 supplied variables in the deduplicated sample
($n = 71,913$), an explicit missingness audit revealed zero missing
values (`NA = 0`).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Conversion Rate Consistency Check for Top Non-USD Currencies
conversion_rates <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(salary_currency %in% c("EUR", "GBP", "CAD")) |>
  mutate(implied_fx_rate = salary_in_usd / salary) |>
  group_by(work_year, salary_currency) |>
  summarise(
    mean_rate = mean(implied_fx_rate),
    min_rate = min(implied_fx_rate),
    max_rate = max(implied_fx_rate),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(across(c(mean_rate, min_rate, max_rate), ~ round(., 4)))

knitr::kable(
  conversion_rates,
  col.names = c("Work Year", "Currency", "Mean Implied FX", "Min FX", "Max FX"),
  caption = "Implied annual exchange conversion consistency (Local Currency to USD)"
)
```

## Years Covered

```{r year-coverage, echo=FALSE}
year_counts <- salaries_analysis %>%

  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),

knitr::kable(
```

The raw dataset spans 2020 through 2025, but density is heavily skewed
toward recent years (2024–2025). An important thing to note is that 2025
will not contain a full calendar year of records as the snapshot was
made in August.

## Countries

```{r geo-coverage, echo=FALSE}
top_employee_countries <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(employee_residence, name = "n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  mutate(
    type = "Employee Residence",
    pct = percent(n / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.01),
    n = comma(n)
  ) %>%
  rename(country_code = employee_residence)

top_company_countries <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(company_location, name = "n") %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  mutate(
    type = "Company Location",
    pct = percent(n / nrow(salaries_analysis), accuracy = 0.01),
    n = comma(n)
  ) %>%
  rename(country_code = company_location)

geo_combined <- bind_rows(top_employee_countries, top_company_countries) |>
  select(type, country_code, n, pct)

knitr::kable(
  geo_combined,
  col.names = c("Dimension", "Country Code", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Top 5 geographical concentrations for employees and employers"
)
```

The dataset is heavily dominated by US geographic concentration where
83.55% of respondents reside in the United States, and 83.64% of
employing companies are based in the U.S.

## Company size composition

```{r size-composition, echo=FALSE}
company_summary <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(company_size, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    company_size = case_when(
      company_size == "S" ~ "Small (<50 employees)",
      company_size == "M" ~ "Medium (50-250 employees)",
      company_size == "L" ~ "Large (>250 employees)"
    ),
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  company_summary,
  col.names = c("Company Size", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Distribution of records by employing firm size"
)
```

The distribution of company size is heavily dominated by Medium-sized
companies (50-250 employees) accounting for 97.5% of all deduplicated
observations ($n=70,110$). Large-sized companies (\>250 employees)
account for 2.2% ($n=1,588$) and Small-sized companies (\<50 employees)
account for 0.3% ($n=215$).

## Remote-status composition

```{r remote-composition, echo=FALSE}
remote_summary <- salaries_analysis %>%
  count(remote_ratio, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    remote_ratio = case_when(
      remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-Site (0% remote)",
      remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid (50% remote)",
      remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully Remote (100% remote)"
    ),
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  remote_summary,
  col.names = c("Remote Policy", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Distribution of records by remote work model"
)
```

`remote_ratio` only takes three values: 0 (on-site), 50 (hybrid), 100
(fully remote) so it lacks detail regarding mandatory in-office days or
flexible hybrid policies. On-site observations dominates the
distribution as it accounts for 75.2% of all deduplicated observations.

## Job title composition

```{r, echo=FALSE}
salaries_analysis <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    title_clean = job_title |> str_to_lower() |> str_squish(),
    role_family = case_when(
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bproduct manager\\b|\\bproduct management\\b|\\bproduct owner\\b|\\bproduct lead\\b")) ~ "Product & Technical Leadership",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata scientist\\b|\\bdata science\\b|\\bdecision scientist\\b|\\bcientista de dados\\b")) ~ "Data Scientist",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bmachine learning\\b|\\bml engineer\\b|\\bml scientist\\b|\\bml researcher\\b|\\bmlops\\b|\\bartificial intelligence\\b|\\bai engineer\\b|\\bai architect\\b|\\bai scientist\\b|\\bgenai\\b|\\bcomputer vision\\b|\\bnlp engineer\\b|\\bllm engineer\\b|\\bdeep learning\\b")) ~ "Machine Learning / AI",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata engineer\\b|\\banalytics engineer\\b|\\bdata architect\\b|\\bdata platform\\b|\\bdata infrastructure\\b|\\bdata pipeline\\b|\\bdataops\\b|\\betl\\b")) ~ "Data Engineering & Architecture",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata analyst\\b|\\bbusiness analyst\\b|\\bproduct analyst\\b|\\binsight analyst\\b|\\bbusiness intelligence\\b|\\bbi\\b|\\btableau\\b|\\bpower bi\\b")) ~ "Data & BI Analyst",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bsoftware\\b|\\bsystems? engineer\\b|\\bplatform engineer\\b|\\bdevops\\b|\\bbackend\\b|\\bfrontend\\b|\\bfull[ -]?stack\\b|\\bcloud engineer\\b")) ~ "Software & Platform Engineering",
      str_detect(title_clean, regex("\\bdata manager\\b|\\bengineering manager\\b|\\bdirector of data\\b|\\bhead of data\\b|\\btechnical project manager\\b")) ~ "Product & Technical Leadership",
      TRUE ~ "Other / unclassified"
    )
  )

role_family_table <- salaries_analysis |>
  count(role_family, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  role_family_table,
  col.names = c("Role Family", "Record Count (n)", "Share of Sample"),
  caption = "Standardized role family categorization logic summary"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
role_family_counts <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified") |>
  count(role_family, sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    prop = n / sum(n),
    role_family = fct_reorder(role_family, prop)
  )

role_family_counts |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prop, y = role_family)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(percent(prop, accuracy = 0.1), " (n = ", comma(n), ")")),
    hjust = -0.05,
    size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
  labs(
    title = "Role-family representation in the analytic sample",
    subtitle = "Share of exact-deduplicated records with a classified role family.",
    x = "Share of classified records",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary survey (Aug 3, 2025). Exact duplicates removed; unclassified titles excluded."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )
```

We assigned 49,270 of 71,913 exact-deduplicated records (68.5%) to six
role families using ordered, specialty-first keyword rules. Titles were
classified only when their text identified a recognizable occupational
function. Generic titles including Engineer, Manager, Analyst,
Developer, Director, and Research Scientist remained unclassified
because the archive contains no job descriptions with which to infer
their function. The 22,643 unclassified records (31.5%) were excluded
from role-family comparisons but retained in analyses that did not
depend on role family.

## Cross-border sparsity

```{r cross-border-sparsity, echo=FALSE}
cross_border_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    geography_type = if_else(
      employee_residence == company_location,
      "Domestic (Same Country)",
      "Cross-Border (Different Countries)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(geography_type) |>
  mutate(
    pct = percent(n / sum(n), accuracy = 0.2),
    n = comma(n)
  )

knitr::kable(
  cross_border_summary,
  col.names = c("Geographic Relationship", "Record Count (n)", "Share"),
  caption = "Comparison of domestic vs. cross-border employment arrangements"
)
```

Records with differing employee-residence and employer-location countries
were too sparse to support robust geographic-arbitrage modeling. Different
countries alone do not establish the employee's precise remote-work setup.
Only 156 of 71,913 distinct records (0.2%) have different recorded
residence and employer countries.

## Audit limits

-   Removing exact duplicates reduced the dataset from 151,445 to 71,913
    records (a 52.5% reduction). Without respondent or posting
    identifiers, we cannot confirm whether the repeats were data
    duplication or distinct people with identical observed value.

-   The archive has no employer name, posting ID, observation date, or
    row-level source to verify individual entries.

-   Record counts represent survey submissions, not employer demand or
    job-opening counts.

-   \`salary_in_usd\` reflects nominal base salary only, not total
    compensation, and is unadjusted for inflation or local purchasing
    power.

-   Remote status is limited to three discrete values (0, 50, 100)
    without detail on hybrid policies.

-   Employee residence and employer location are recorded at the country
    level, omitting city- or regional-level variation.

-   Cross-border employer/employee pairs (0.22% of unique records) are
    too sparse for reliable comparison.

-   All observed differences across roles, experience levels, and
    company sizes are descriptive associations only.

-   The data source also has the majority of salary observations in 2024
    to 2025. This means that there are limited time series analysis
    opportunities.

# 2. Compensation landscape

```{r, echo=FALSE}
family_audit <- salaries_analysis |>
  group_by(role_family) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    share = n / nrow(salaries_analysis),
    unique_titles = n_distinct(job_title),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(median_salary))

family_audit |>
  mutate(
    share = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n),
    unique_titles = comma(unique_titles),
    across(
      c(median_salary, lower_quartile, upper_quartile),
      ~ dollar(.x, accuracy = 1)
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Role Family", "Count (n)", "Share", "Unique Titles", "Median Salary", "25th Percentile", "75th Percentile"),
    caption = "Coverage and compensation summaries under the final role-family rules (deduplicated sample)"
  )
```

## The Compensation Distribution & Outlier Dashboard

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Identify high earners for annotation
high_earner_threshold <- 500000

salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = salary_in_usd, y = fct_reorder(role_family, salary_in_usd, median))) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "lightblue", color = "slategray", outlier.alpha = 0.2, outlier.size = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = high_earner_threshold, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 520000, y = 0.8, 
    label = "Extreme Outlier Threshold ($500k+)", 
    color = "firebrick", hjust = 0, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5
  ) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = label_dollar(),
    breaks = c(30000, 100000, 300000, 500000, 1000000)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "High-Tier Compensation Variance and Extreme Outliers Across Role Domains",
    subtitle = "Log10 scale boxplots isolating extreme compensation outliers (≥ $500,000 threshold).",
    x = "Annual Reported Base Salary in Nominal USD (log scale)",
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Deduplicated analytic sample."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

Across the deduplicated sample ($n = 71,913$), reported base salaries
displayed right-skewness and extreme high-end outliers across all
technical categories. Therefore, we decided to use medians and
interquartile ranges (IQR) as the primary metrics for central tendency
and spread.

Machine Learning / AI displayed the highest median reported salary at
\$170,042 ($n = 6,144$, 8.5% of sample; IQR: \$125,375–\$226,000).
Product & Technical Leadership at \$163,925 ( $n = 3,381$, 4.7%; IQR: \$114,500–\$224,000) and
Software & Platform Engineering at \$159,000 ( $n = 8,149$, 11.3%; IQR: \$117,000–\$210,985)
follow closely as top-tier compensation drivers. Data Scientist roles
report a median salary of \$142,000 ($n = 7,356$, 10.2%; IQR:
\$100,000–\$191,500), closely followed by Data Engineering &
Architecture at \$139,400 ($n = 9,903$, 13.8%; IQR: \$99,800–\$186,000).
Data & BI Analyst records the lowest compensation baseline among defined
role families at \$100,000 ($n = 9,506$, 13.2%; IQR:
\$72,500–\$136,000), with a difference of \$70,042 from the ML/AI median
(a 41.2% lower baseline).

# 3. Career and market signals

## Client Question 1: How do compensation trajectories differ across career levels, and what is the financial return when progressing through tiers?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Summarize salary medians by role family and experience level
role_experience_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified") |>
  group_by(role_family, experience_level) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    experience_level = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")
    )
  )

# Calculate adjacent-tier dollar and percentage progression
career_progression <- role_experience_summary |>
  arrange(role_family, experience_level) |>
  group_by(role_family) |>
  mutate(
    previous_level = lag(experience_level),
    previous_median = lag(median_salary),
    dollar_increase = median_salary - previous_median,
    percent_increase = 100 * (median_salary - previous_median) / previous_median
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
role_experience_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = experience_level, y = median_salary, color = role_family, group = role_family)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Reported salary rises across career tiers in every role family",
    subtitle = "Median annual reported base salary by experience tier and role family.",
    x = "Experience Tier",
    y = "Median Base Salary (USD)",
    color = "Role Family",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary survey (Aug 3, 2025). Exact duplicates removed."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

```

This line plot displays the median annual reported base salary (USD) on
the y-axis plotted across sequential experience tiers (Entry, Mid,
Senior, Executive) on the x-axis, broken down by six distinct role
families separated by different color lines. Machine Learning / AI
($\$110,000$ Entry) and Product & Technical Leadership ($\$124,800$
Entry) start as the highest salary benchmarks and maintain top-tier
positioning through the Executive level ($\$205,000$+). Software &
Platform Engineering shows the steepest slope, ascending from an Entry
baseline of $~\$106,590$ to the highest Executive median in the dataset
($\$210,000$+). Data & BI Analyst remains the lowest-paid role family at
every career stage, starting at $\$81,000$ (Entry) and ending at
$\$144,800$ (Executive), trailing ML/AI Executive levels by over
$\$60,000$.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
career_progression |>
  filter(!is.na(previous_level)) |>
  mutate(
    transition = factor(
      paste(previous_level, "to", experience_level),
      levels = c("Entry to Mid", "Mid to Senior", "Senior to Executive")
    ),
    role_family = fct_reorder(role_family, percent_increase, .fun = mean)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = transition, y = role_family, fill = percent_increase)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(percent_increase, 1), "%\n+$", comma(dollar_increase))),
    size = 3.8,
    color = "#1F1F1F"
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "gray95", high = "steelblue", labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Salary gains between adjacent career tiers vary substantially by role",
    subtitle = "Percentage and dollar differences between adjacent median salary levels.",
    x = "Adjacent Tier Transition",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Percent Difference",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary survey (Aug 3, 2025). Compares separate experience groups, not longitudinal raises."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

This plot displays a heatmap matrix mapping role families against
adjacent career tier transitions. Each cell displays both the percentage
salary difference and the absolute dollar gain, shaded by the magnitude
of the percentage increase. Engineering & Architecture yields the
highest early-career (Entry to Mid) promotion gain at +48.5%
(+$\$38,800$), followed by Data Scientist at +36.2% (+$\$32,001$). Data
Scientist leads mid-career (Mid to Senior) progression with a +32.8%
(+$\$39,549$) median step-up. Lastly, Data Engineering & Architecture
records the largest absolute executive expansion at +30.0%
(+$\$45,000$), followed by Data and BI Analyst at +23% (+$\$27,056$) and
Data Science Leadership at +18.9% (+$\$30,250$).

### Key findings

The largest adjacent-tier differences in observed median salary occur in
Data Engineering & Architecture and Data Science at earlier career stages.
These are comparisons between groups of records, **not observed raises
for individual workers**. They provide directional benchmarks rather than
prescriptions for employer compensation budgets.

## Client Question 2: Is there a measurable remote work premium or remote penalty?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
remote_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = case_when(
      remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-site",
      remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid",
      remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully remote"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(remote_status) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    share = n() / nrow(salaries_analysis),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    lower_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    upper_quartile = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    share = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1),
    n = comma(n),
    across(c(median_salary, lower_quartile, upper_quartile), ~ dollar(., accuracy = 1))
  )

knitr::kable(
  remote_summary,
  col.names = c("Remote Status", "Count (n)", "Share", "Median Salary", "25th Percentile", "75th Percentile"),
  caption = "Unadjusted salary statistics by remote work arrangement"
)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = factor(
      case_when(
        remote_ratio == 0 ~ "On-site",
        remote_ratio == 50 ~ "Hybrid",
        remote_ratio == 100 ~ "Fully remote"
      ),
      levels = c("On-site", "Hybrid", "Fully remote")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = remote_status, y = salary_in_usd, fill = remote_status)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = label_dollar()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("slategray2", "goldenrod2", "steelblue3")) +
  labs(
    title = "Raw salary distributions overlap across remote work arrangements",
    subtitle = "Unadjusted comparisons do not control for role mix, seniority, firm size, or work year.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Annual Base Salary in Nominal USD (log scale)",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Deduplicated sample."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The plot shows a side-by-side boxplot display and accompanying summary
table comparing reported annual base salary distributions in nominal USD
(on a log scale) across three remote work categories: On-site (0%),
Hybrid (50%), and Fully Remote (100%). Fully Remote roles report an
unadjusted median base salary of $\$140,000$ (IQR:
$\$100,000$–$\$187,200$), closely matching On-site roles at $\$138,300$
(IQR: $\$95,300$–$\$192,890$). Hybrid roles represent a sparse,
lower-paid subset (0.5% of records, $\$69,999$ median). Raw comparisons
fail to show a clear difference between the distributions of on-site and
fully remote salaries but justifies the need for multiple regression.

### Regression Analysis

To estimate an adjusted association between remote work and salary,
we fit a log-linear model controlling for role family, experience level,
company size, and work year. We use log salary to reduce the influence of large values
and address some right-skewness, while checking model diagnostics for
remaining assumption violations (see [Appendix](#appendix)). Our main
covariate of interest is remote status as we want to determine whether
remote employees face a compensation premium. The model controls for the
other potential confounding variables including role family controlling
for pay variation across different fields, experience level controlling
for difference in pay depending on seniority, company size controlling
for wage premiums based on small, medium, and large companies, and
lastly work year controlling for changing environmental factors over
time. We only consider the six role families we have previously created
as well as only on-site and fully remote observations. Categorical
predictors are parametrized using dummy indicator variables.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
remote_model_data <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(
    remote_ratio %in% c(0, 100),
    role_family != "Other / unclassified"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    remote_status = factor(if_else(remote_ratio == 0, "On-site", "Fully remote"), levels = c("On-site", "Fully remote")),
    experience_level = factor(experience_level, levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"), labels = c("Entry", "Mid", "Senior", "Executive")),
    company_size = factor(company_size, levels = c("S", "M", "L"), labels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large")),
    work_year = factor(work_year)
  )

remote_salary_model <- lm(
  log(salary_in_usd) ~ remote_status + role_family + experience_level + company_size + work_year,
  data = remote_model_data
)

# Lecture-native regression summary conversion using base R coef()
model_coefs <- summary(remote_salary_model)$coefficients |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = "Term") |>
  mutate(
    `Estimate (log)` = round(Estimate, 4),
    `Implied % Change` = percent(exp(Estimate) - 1, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Std. Error` = round(`Std. Error`, 4),
    `p-value` = if_else(`Pr(>|t|)` < 0.001, "< 0.001", as.character(round(`Pr(>|t|)`, 3)))
  ) |>
  select(Term, `Estimate (log)`, `Implied % Change`, `Std. Error`, `p-value`)

knitr::kable(
  head(model_coefs, 10),
  caption = "Log-linear salary regression model coefficients (selected key variables)"
)
```

Conditional on the included role-family, experience, firm-size, and year
indicators, the fully remote coefficient is estimated at $\hat{\beta} = -0.0073$,
roughly a **-0.7%** association compared with on-site records. The
estimate is not statistically significant ($t = -1.47$, $p = 0.141$);
the reported 95% interval for the transformed percentage difference is
approximately **-1.69% to +0.24%**. The data do not provide sufficient
evidence of a nonzero conditional association at $\alpha = 0.05$.
They do not prove pay equivalence.

The model also shows large conditional differences in reported salaries
across career levels and role families; these are associations, not
causal salary premiums.

### Key findings

In this specification, the observed fully remote difference is small
and not statistically significant after adjustment. The result should
not be used alone to set remote-work compensation policy: geography,
selection into remote work, unobserved company characteristics, and
non-salary compensation may also matter.


## Client Question 3: Where are salaries growing, and which specific roles and company sizes present the best opportunities for executive recruiting?

```{r, echo=FALSE}
career_size_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  mutate(

      levels = c("EN", "MI", "SE", "EX"),

    ),

      levels = c("S", "M", "L"),
      labels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large")

  ) |>
  group_by(company_size_label, experience_tier) |>

    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),

career_size_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = experience_tier, y = company_size_label, fill = median_salary)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  # Dynamic text color: black text on bright yellow tiles, white text on dark tiles
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = dollar(median_salary),
      color = median_salary > 170000
    ),
    fontface = "bold",
    size = 3.8,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "white", "TRUE" = "black")) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "C",
    labels = label_dollar(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")
  ) +
  guides(
    fill = guide_colorbar(
      title = "Median Salary",
      title.position = "top",
      title.hjust = 0.5,
      barwidth = grid::unit(12, "lines"),
      barheight = grid::unit(0.6, "lines")
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Median salary rises by career tier across employer sizes",
    subtitle = "Medium-sized companies show higher executive pay baselines ($190k) than large firms ($141k).",
    x = "Experience Tier",
    y = "Employer Size",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net salary snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). Deduplicated sample."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    legend.margin = margin(t = 10, b = 5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 1, margin = margin(t = 10))
  )
```

The figure above is a 2D heatmap that illustrates median base salaries
across three company sizes (y-axis) and four seniority levels (x-axis),
with color intensity reflecting salary scale. While pay generally
increases with seniority, company size heavily influences peak executive
earnings. Mid-sized businesses (50–250 employees) lead the market with a
median executive salary of $\$190,000$, significantly outperforming
large corporations ($\$140,973$) and small businesses ($\$120,000$).
Because almost all records come from medium-sized employers, these
between-size comparisons are descriptive and should not be generalized
to the employer market without checking group sample sizes and selection
bias.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
year_role_summary <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(role_family != "Other / unclassified", work_year %in% c(2024, 2025)) |>
  group_by(work_year, role_family) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

year_role_summary |>
  mutate(
    work_year_label = factor(
      work_year,
      levels = c(2024, 2025),
      labels = c("2024 Full Year", "2025 Partial\n(thru Aug 3)")
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = work_year_label, y = median_salary, color = role_family, group = role_family)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Salary benchmarks across most role families soft in partial 2025",
    subtitle = "Comparison of median annual base salary between 2024 full year and 2025 YTD snapshot.",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Median Base Salary (USD)",
    color = "Role Family",
    caption = "Source: aijobs.net snapshot (Aug 3, 2025). 2025 represents an incomplete calendar year."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

This figure compares cross-sectional medians of annual nominal base salary
across six role families for full-year
2024 to partial 2025 (snapshot through August 3, 2025). Comparing 2024
full-year benchmarks to partial 2025 entries reveals that Product &
Technical Leadership is the only domain showing clear pay expansion
(rising toward $\$166,000$). Machine Learning / AI holds steady at the
top market threshold ($\sim\$175,000$), while foundational analytics and
core engineering roles show mild softening in partial 2025. Even though
Machine Learning / AI roles require smaller budget allocations for
salary increases from senior to executive levels, the roles have the
greatest salaries overall. Additionally, even though Data & BI Analyst
roles offer the highest relative returns on senior-career promotion
budgets, their overall salary benchmarks tend to be significantly lower
than other roles.

### Key findings

The sample suggests comparatively high medians in some medium-company
and leadership groups, but it cannot establish employer willingness to
pay or future recruitment demand. The 2025 records cover only part of
the year, so comparisons with 2024 should be read as snapshot contrasts,
not sustained year-over-year growth rates.

# 4. Recruiting Playbook

## Target Employer

As part of the class consulting scenario, the team selected **Walmart
Global Tech** as a *proposed* enterprise employer for a hypothetical
executive-search pitch. The aim was to connect the descriptive salary
analysis to a real-world technology workforce case study.

The supplied salary dataset contains **no company names or job openings**,
so these results cannot independently establish Walmart's specific hiring
needs, recruitment challenges, salary bands, vendor budgets, or willingness
to pay recruiting fees. Public company information discussed in the
original presentation is contextual; any actual sales recommendation
would require current, independently verified employer-specific research.

## Priority Roles and Experience Tiers

Libeccio will focus its sales and recruiting efforts exclusively on
Senior (SE) and Executive (EX) roles in three specific areas. These
focus areas match the highest-paying, fastest-growing roles in our
dataset and align directly with Walmart's technical roles.

**Product & Technical Leadership**, **Machine Learning / AI**, and
**Software & Platform Engineering** were chosen for illustrative
recruiting pipelines because the role-family summaries show high
reported medians. For example, Machine Learning / AI reports a median
of about \$170,042 across experience tiers, while the Software &
Platform Engineering summary shows a large Senior-to-Executive median
salary gap. These are broad survey categories, not employer-specific
role descriptions or observed promotion raises.

As the needs of Walmart evolve over the years, Libeccio can become a
trusted partner and develop a personalized relationship with Walmart. By
maintaining relationships with qualified senior candidates and adapting
to the needs of Walmart's technical priorities, we intend to form a
reliable partnership with them rather than maximizing the short-term
value on placement.

## Salary Benchmarks

These metrics summarize annual base salaries across Libeccio’s target
roles.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Directional Compensation Benchmarks for Priority Target Roles
priority_benchmarks <- salaries_analysis |>
  filter(
    role_family %in% c(
      "Product & Technical Leadership",
      "Machine Learning / AI",
      "Software & Platform Engineering"
    ),
    experience_level %in% c("SE", "EX")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    experience_tier = factor(
      experience_level,
      levels = c("SE", "EX"),
      labels = c("Senior", "Executive")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(role_family, experience_tier) |>
  summarise(
    sample_size = n(),
    median_salary = median(salary_in_usd, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25 = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75 = quantile(salary_in_usd, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(role_family, experience_tier) |>
  mutate(
    sample_size = comma(sample_size),
    across(c(median_salary, q25, q75), ~ dollar(., accuracy = 1))
  )

knitr::kable(
  priority_benchmarks,
  col.names = c("Role Family", "Experience Tier", "Sample Size (n)", "Median Base Salary", "25th Percentile", "75th Percentile"),
  caption = "Directional Compensation Benchmarks for Target Sourcing Priorities (Source: aijobs.net frozen snapshot, Aug. 3, 2025; deduplicated N = 71,913)"
)
```

These sample medians offer directional reference points for the
hypothetical search strategy. They do not reveal Walmart-specific salary
bands, hiring budgets, or what a recruiter could charge.

## Search Strategy

The team's original proposal distinguished core, selective,
experimental, and deferred recruiting opportunities. As an analytical
extension, a recruiter could use role-family medians to **prioritize
questions** about senior and executive compensation, while validating
current demand, location, equity compensation, and exact titles against
employer-specific sources before making commitments.

The analysis does not estimate search fees, hiring costs, or causal
salary gains, and the absence of a statistically significant remote
coefficient should not be interpreted as permission to ignore geographic
compensation differences.

## Next Data Source

This snapshot reports base salary, not total compensation. It does not
include stock grants, sign-on bonuses, annual bonuses, or other benefits.
For a production-grade recruiting study, the next step would be to
incorporate a transparently sourced total-compensation dataset, as well
as current employer-specific pay bands and job demand. Any commercial
data source would need to be assessed for coverage and licensing.
